Anthropic’s Sonnet 5.5 costs half of what Opus 5.5 does, thinks longer on max effort, and its builds still break once Blender hits play.

A still frame flatters both models. Only the timeline shows which one understood how the object is meant to move.

> BRIEF - one identical object description, both models set to max effort
> BUILD - mesh, materials and hierarchy assembled in Blender with no human edits
> PLAY - every rig run through a full animation instead of judged on frame one
> CLOCK - wall time and spend logged for each build, prompt to final file

On frame one the outputs were hard to tell apart: matching silhouettes, clean topology, sensible material slots.

Motion split them within seconds. Sonnet’s joints bent where the object never would, and weights bled into rigid parts.

Max effort did not close that gap. Sonnet spent more time reasoning on every build and still landed a weaker rig.

Effort is a dial for search time, not for capacity. Turning it up let Sonnet look longer, never deeper.

Static work is where Sonnet makes sense. Props and scenery that never move came back close enough at half the bill.

So the routing rule writes itself: anything that moves goes to Opus, anything that sits still can go to Sonnet.

Scene by scene, with timings and the real cost of each build, the full scorecard follows.

Opus 5.5 being “2x more expensive” is one of those facts that dies the second you run a long agent loop

[the loop changes the math]

1. at 20K context, Opus is still 1.88x Sonnet per turn

2. at 150K, that falls to 1.49x. by 400K, it is only 1.26x

3. the reason is cache. both models pay the same $0.20 / 1M for cache reads, so old context stops widening the bill

4. the ugly part is switching late. drag 300K of failed context into Opus and you spend $1.50 just rebuilding cache

5. catch the failure around turn 6 and hand off 20K instead. that costs about $0.10

at 150K, 30 Sonnet turns cost $1.76

20 Opus turns cost $1.75

the real optimization is not “use the cheaper model”

it is knowing when to stop paying for the wrong one ↓

hits.text:
OpenAI cracked a batch of supposedly quantum-only problems on a regular laptop, and the promised advantage disappeared with them.

Speed had nothing to do with it. The model hunted for hidden structure that lets an ordinary machine take the same shortcut.

> CLAIM - every published problem pitched as beyond classical reach, gathered in one place
> STRIP - each one reduced to the math it actually asks for, with the pitch removed
> HUNT - the model searches for low-rank and sampling structure a laptop can exploit
> BUILD - a classical algorithm written for every problem where that structure turned up
> RACE - both approaches run on the same instance sizes and timed side by side
> KEEP - only the problems that survive the race stay on the quantum list

A surprising share of the list did not make it through. Several fell to careful sampling on one ordinary CPU.

Their speedup leaned on an assumption, not on physics: that the classical side could only read data one entry at a time.

Give the laptop the same access the quantum machine was granted, and the gap closes.
